faq.a: No; type 1 diabetes requires insulin because there is no endogenous insulin production.
faq.q: Can oral agents be used in type 1 diabetes?

faq.a: It lowers hepatic glucose output, improves insulin sensitivity, is inexpensive, and has low hypoglycaemia risk.
faq.q: Why is metformin preferred as first‑line?

faq.a: Stop the sulfonylurea, treat with glucose, and consider switching to metformin or a safer agent.
faq.q: What to do if a patient develops hypoglycaemia on a sulfonylurea?

ai.title: Oral Hypoglycaemic Agents
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs) lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes by various mechanisms. In low‑resource settings clinicians must choose agents that are affordable, safe, and usable without extensive monitoring.

b: Used only when patient has T2DM, not type 1 diabetes.
Require documented hyperglycaemia on at least two occasions.
sections.p: OHAs are non‑insulin medicines taken by mouth to reduce hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Diagnosis of T2DM follows WHO criteria: fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2‑hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL, or HbA1c ≥6.5 %.

b: Higher HbA1c pushes earlier combination therapy.
Complications (retinopathy, nephropathy) dictate tighter control.
sections.p: Severity is staged by glycaemic control and complications, not by a formal OHA stage. Use the WHO/IDF risk stratification: low (HbA1c <7 %), moderate (7‑9 %), high (>9 %).

b: Obesity and sedentary lifestyle.
Chronic infections (HIV, TB) and antiretroviral therapy.
Use of traditional herbal remedies that impair glucose metabolism.
sections.p: Hyperglycaemia prompting OHA use arises from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. In East Africa common contributors include:

b: Random glucose >200 mg/dL with symptoms.
HbA1c ≥6.5 % on laboratory testing.
sections.p: Patients present with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue. In low‑resource settings, presentation may be delayed, with complications such as foot ulcers or visual loss already evident.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment or alternative bedside methods.

t.b: Is the patient hyperglycaemic? — ≥126 mg/dL confirms diabetes.
What is long‑term control? — ≥6.5 % indicates diabetes; trends guide therapy intensity.
Can the patient safely receive metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors? — eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² for metformin.
Are there contraindications to certain OHAs? — ALT/AST >3× ULN cautions use of thiazolidinediones.

b: Lactic acidosis risk with metformin: renal failure, sepsis, dehydration.
Severe hypoglycaemia with sulfonylureas or meglitinides.
Heart failure exacerbation with thiazolidinediones.
sections.p: Identify patients at risk of severe adverse events or treatment failure.

b: Metformin first‑line: reduces hepatic glucose output, weight neutral, low hypoglycaemia risk; avoid if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Sulfonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide) if metformin contraindicated; watch for hypoglycaemia, especially in malnourished patients.
SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin) when renal function ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m²; provide cardiovascular benefit but risk genital infections; may be costly.
Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone) for insulin resistance when heart failure absent; monitor for fluid retention.
Avoid meglitinides in patients with erratic meals; they have short action but higher cost.
sections.p: Start with lifestyle modification, then add the most appropriate OHA based on efficacy, safety, cost, and organ function.

b: Check fasting glucose or HbA1c every 3‑6 months.
Assess renal function before each metformin refill.
Screen annually for retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy.
sections.p: Regular monitoring of glycaemia, renal and hepatic function, and complications is essential.

b: Insulin: injectable, required in type 1 diabetes or advanced T2DM.
Herbal glucose‑lowering agents: lack robust evidence and may interact with OHAs.
sections.p: Distinguish OHAs from insulin therapy and from non‑diabetic glucose‑lowering measures.

b: Fasting glucose can be normal in early morning but post‑prandial spikes persist; always assess HbA1c or 2‑hour OGTT.
Renal function estimated by creatinine alone may over‑estimate eGFR in low‑muscle‑mass patients; consider cystatin C if available.
sections.p: Certain laboratory or bedside findings may give a false sense of control.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting suggesting metformin‑associated lactic acidosis.
Rapidly worsening heart failure after starting a thiazolidinedione.
